column2: What reference identifies a reusable workflow in another GitHub repository?
column3: owner/repo/.github/workflows/file.yml@ref, with source access and Actions policies permitting use.

column2: What balances stable GitHub reusable-component consumption with receiving fixes?
column3: Pin a reviewed immutable revision, then update that pin through reviewed and tested changes.

column2: Should shared logic that defines several jobs use a composite action or reusable workflow?
column3: A reusable workflow; a composite action runs steps inside a caller's job.

column2: What minimum GitHub token permission commonly supports reading repository content?
column3: contents: read. Grant additional permissions only for operations that need them.

column2: In a GitHub permissions map, what happens to permissions not specified once some are specified?
column3: They are set to none, except any documented special cases; review the complete job requirements.

column2: Why does a GitHub job that creates an issue need more than contents read access?
column3: Issue creation needs issues: write; permissions are scoped by capability.

column2: Why put a production credential in a protected GitHub environment rather than a general repository secret?
column3: Environment secrets are available only to jobs using that environment after its configured protections pass.

column2: How does GitHub OIDC obtain cloud credentials?
column3: The job requests a GitHub identity token; the cloud validates trusted claims and issues short-lived credentials for an authorised identity.

column2: Does id-token: write itself grant Azure deployment permissions?
column3: No. It allows requesting an OIDC token; cloud trust and resource authorisation are separate.

column2: Why pin a GitHub action to a full commit SHA rather than only a tag?
column3: A tag can move; the commit SHA fixes the selected revision. Review and update the pinned code separately.

column2: Is a third-party action automatically safe because its organisation is allowlisted?
column3: No. Review the action's code, dependencies and required privileges, and pin an approved revision.

column2: Why is interpolating a pull-request title directly into a GitHub run script unsafe?
column3: The title can contain executable syntax. Pass it as data through an environment variable or action input and handle it safely.

column2: What should an untrusted pull-request job be unable to access?
column3: Deployment credentials, privileged tokens, sensitive networks and persistent trusted runner state.

column2: What does a configured GitHub environment approval gate protect?
column3: Jobs referencing that environment wait for its protections; secrets become available only after those protections pass.

column2: If a GitHub environment lists several required reviewers, must all approve?
column3: No. One listed reviewer approval is sufficient; configure self-review and bypass restrictions as needed.

column2: When should a team evaluate GitHub larger runners?
column3: When standard runners cannot meet measured compute, networking or administration needs; verify plan, OS and feature availability.

column2: What must a self-hosted GitHub runner lifecycle cover beyond registration?
column3: Patching, access restrictions, monitoring, cleanup and deregistration when retired.

column2: Does marking a GitHub runner ephemeral automatically wipe its host?
column3: No. It limits runner registration to one job; the operator must destroy or clean the underlying environment.

column2: What does Actions Runner Controller manage?
column3: Kubernetes-based self-hosted GitHub runner infrastructure and scaling.

column2: How does an ARC runner scale set respond to queued jobs?
column3: Its listener observes available work and requests runner capacity within configured scaling bounds.

column2: Does private network connectivity make a runner safe for arbitrary pull requests?
column3: No. It can expose private services to the job; restrict both execution trust and network reachability.

column2: How can GitHub runner groups restrict a sensitive runner pool?
column3: Allow only selected repositories and, where supported and configured, selected workflows.

column2: Which GitHub enterprise Actions policies help control external executable dependencies?
column3: Policies restricting allowed actions and reusable workflows, combined with appropriate pinning and permission controls.

column2: Which GitHub setting enables extra step diagnostic logs?
column3: Set ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG to true as a secret or variable; protect diagnostic output from sensitive data.

column2: How do GitHub run logs differ from job summaries?
column3: Logs record execution detail; job summaries present curated Markdown results through GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY.

column2: Should a release artifact be treated as a disposable dependency cache?
column3: No. Cache accelerates reconstruction; a release artifact is a specific output requiring traceability and suitable retention.

column2: What inputs matter when estimating GitHub Actions cost?
column3: Current plan allowances, runner type and usage, storage consumption and retention, plus infrastructure costs for self-hosted execution.

column2: Why can a GitHub job queue even when some runners appear idle?
column3: It may lack an eligible runner, hit concurrency limits, or wait on a concurrency group or prerequisite.

column2: Which GitHub CLI command displays failed-job logs for run 12345?
column3: gh run view 12345 --log-failed in the intended repository context.

column2: Which evidence distinguishes slow CI from unauthorised configuration change?
column3: Run timing and failure metrics explain performance; audit events and version history attribute configuration changes.
